newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - From the Beehive - The dogged defence of NZ.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - From the Beehive - The dogged defence of NZ.

text.p: WELLINGTON, July 25 - Loose cannons, mongrels, "dingoistic bureaucrats" and rows over defence spending.
Ah, the old Anzac spirit lives on.
If the United Kingdom and the United States are divided by a common language, Australia and New Zealand are united by their common rivalry.
From the New Zealand side it's most plainly manifested in sport. You sometimes get the feeling synchronised swimming would develop mass appeal if Kiwis could beat Aussies at it.
There is a T-shirt on sale here which seems to best sum up the NZ view of Australian sport. It reads: "I support New Zealand, and whoever is playing against Australia".

So in a week when the All Blacks (EXTREMELY tired from a famous victory over South Africa last week) go to the mecca of Australian sport, the Melbourne Cricket Ground, to play for the symbol of trans-Tasman rugby supremacy -- the Bledisloe Cup -- it wouldn't have taken much to inflame passions here.
A series of leaked reports critical of New Zealand's leaders, its Pacific Island neighbours and its willingness to spend on defence was more than enough to do the trick.

OK, so the overwhelming majority of New Zealanders thinks "The Loose Cannon" aka Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters is not a great leader. And OK, some also think that since the end of the cold war and the demise of ANZUS, money spent on frigates would be better put into reducing waiting lists, class sizes and social problems.
But hearing it from big brother across the ditch?
Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare will have lost no support with his description of those responsible for the report on Peters as "mongrels".

But with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, Peters and Finance Minister Bill Birch all in Australia this weekend for the rugby (and some working sessions with their counterparts) differences over defence spending will not have been helped by the public airing -- although in private NZ ministers have been in no doubt about Australia's view.
Bolger this week in the House reiterated the NZ government stance on defence spending -- that the current defence review must be completed before any decisions are made.
But that review hides a lurking problem within the coalition which has its roots in NZ First's desire to see more social spending as its means of branding itself and "making the difference".

In National there is a "hawkish" element, led by Defence Minister Paul East and growing in influence, which is already putting some thought into where the capital expenditure on defence will come from.

There is not enough in the current budgeted capex and Birch has already flagged the first priority for capital clawed back from the SOEs will be schools and hospitals, leaving debt repayment and defence further back in the queue.
There are suggestions some of the present Leander-class frigates could be sold to help defray the costs and thus help "sell" the spending on extra frigates to the doves.

While NZ First went into the election without a defence policy, the coalition agreement agreed to the review of spending "acknowledging there is no commitment to purchase the third and fourth frigates".
That had all the earmarks of an NZ First initiative. But even within NZ First there is unlikely to be a single view.
Whip Ron Mark is ex-army and the heavy weighting of Maori in the armed forces makes it hard to say whether more spending would necessarily be unpopular with NZ First's Maori power base.
The first stage of the defence review, looking at overall strategy, will be with ministers in early August.

The next phase will be a decision on equipment including whether to buy third or fourth Anzac frigates. That must be made by November if NZ is to get them at the fixed 1988 price. One seems likely, two would be a surprise.
Yet is just possible NZ could buy them for less by not exercising the fixed price option, and that could open a window for some further delay.
-- Wellington newsroom 64-4 473 4746
